name: Decentralization
summary: Decentralization is the transfer of authority, responsibility and resources for public decisions from a central government to lower or local bodies, and the decentralist tradition (Kohr, Schumacher, Sale) argues that bigness is the source of social ills and that power should be kept small and close to the people it affects. The governance literature treats it as a family of forms (deconcentration, delegation, devolution; political, administrative, fiscal, economic), while decentralist writers on the left and right differ on what local communities may do with that power. Its sources speak chiefly to where power should sit, so most other questions are left open.

scope: The principle that public authority and decisions should move away from a central body to lower, local or smaller units, as defined in the governance literature on decentralization (Rondinelli, Cheema) and as argued by the decentralist writers whom McClaughry's introduction to decentralism names as its core (Kohr, Schumacher, Sale). It covers political decentralization and the decentralist case for human-scale polities. It excludes federalism, localism, subsidiarity, anarchism and secessionism as separate subjects, whose sources are not used here, and the technical senses of the word in computing, management and monetary systems.

aliases.quote: Centralisation is mainly an idea of order; decentralisation, one of freedom.

keyFigures.name: Leopold Kohr
keyFigures.role: Austrian economist whose The Breakdown of Nations argued that bigness causes social misery and that large states should be broken up.

keyFigures.name: E. F. Schumacher
keyFigures.role: Author of Small Is Beautiful, who popularised Kohr's human-scale ideas.

keyFigures.name: Kirkpatrick Sale
keyFigures.role: Author of Human Scale (1980), described as close to a classic of decentralist thought.

notes: Sources are few because decentralization is a principle about where power sits, not a full programme; the governance literature (s1, s2) is largely value-neutral and says that either centralized or decentralized arrangements can work, and McClaughry (s3) says decentralism is not a defined philosophy and splits into a liberal and a conservative form, left decentralists accepting central ground rules where right decentralists do not. Positions on social, cultural and economic questions are therefore null. Themes searched: definitions and forms (Rondinelli, Cheema), the decentralist canon (McClaughry, Kohr), Tocqueville on administrative centralization (Democracy in America vol. 1, Project Gutenberg, read but not cited because no defining source ties that work to the subject), Schumacher's chapter on large-scale organisation, subsidiarity in Quadragesimo Anno (not used: a separate subject), and the libertarianism.org entry (blocked by a bot check). No missing statement is listed: the defining positions (local decision-making, smallness of polities, regional self-government) are covered by decide-locally, keep-public-institutions-small and the regional statements.
